To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

neonatal anti-Ia antibody treatment results in a specific defect in the development of I-restricted cytotoxic T cells, and this defect is due to interference with the process of Ia recognition and education of T cells in the thymic microenvironment.

in vivo treatment of neonates with monoclonal anti-Ia antibodies results in the abrogation of I-restricted CTL responses, and that the mechanism of this defect is due to interference with the development of Ia-recognizing T helper cells.
in vivo treatment of neonatally immunized mice with anti-I-A antibodies interferes with the development of Ia-restricted T cell responses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the early development of T cells and shows that Ia-encoded products may be involved in the education of Ia-restricted T cell clones.
the early differentiation of the immune system and the role of Ia-encoded gene products in the development of T cells.
the development of the T lymphocyte repertoire.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the in vivo treatment of neonates with anti-I-A antibodies results in the absence of Ia-specific helper cells and a reduced expression of I-A in the thymic cortex and the spleen, thus interfering with the development of I-A-restricted T cells.
anti-I-A antibodies interfere with the development of Ia-restricted T cells by blocking the interaction of precursor T cells with Ia-positive elements in the thymic environment.
the anti-I-Ak treatment interferes with the development of I-Ak-restricted T cells in the thymic microenvironment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ia antigens are required for development of I-A- and I-E-recognizing T helper cells and that this process is mediated through Ia-bearing elements in the thymic microenvironment.
Ia antigens are required for the development of Ia-restricted T cells, and that the Ia molecules involved in this process are Ia antigens expressed on the thymic epithelium.
the I region of the H-2 complex is involved in the development of Ia-restricted T helper cells, but is not involved in the development or maturation of K/D- restricted T cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the development of T cells specific for Ia-encoded products is a complex phenomenon involving the thymic microenvironment and the peripheral microenvironment, as well as the interaction of Ia-positive elements with Ia-recognizing T helper cells.
the T cell repertoire is established in the thymic environment and is not a random process.
Ia-positive thymic elements are required for the development of Ia-restricted T cells in the neonate.
